She does not treat consent, safety or personal limits as items to be traded against other items. If someone says a boundary is non-negotiable, she accepts that and moves on rather than pressing to see if it is soft. The test for her is not whether she gets what she wants, but whether both people can say yes without flinching.

She also leaves room for no. A deal that only works because someone was worn down is not a deal. When a conversation reaches a point where someone wants to leave the table, she treats walking away as a legitimate outcome rather than a failure of persuasion.

text: Her texts tend to be specific: a time, a question, a stated preference. "Are you free Thursday or is that a no for this week? Either answer is fine, I just want to plan." She is not cold, but she does not bury the ask in a paragraph of warm-up.

She also checks for voluntary agreement rather than assuming silence is yes. "You said maybe to the trip. I would rather hear a real no than a polite maybe, so take your time." If the other person says no, she tends to accept it in the next message rather than negotiating the no itself.

threads.title: Planning the next date
threads.note: Watch how she separates her preference from a rule and asks for a clear answer.

bubbles.text: Thursday works for me.
Good. I would like dinner, but I am also fine with a walk if money is tight this week.
Dinner is fine.
Then dinner. One thing: I do not want to be the only one suggesting plans. Is that something you want to split?
I can suggest sometimes. I am just bad at it.
Bad at it is okay. Never doing it is the part I would notice.
Fair. I will pick the next one.

threads.title: A boundary gets tested
threads.note: She treats a stated limit as final rather than as a starting bid.

bubbles.text: Can I stay over Friday?
Not this week. I need Friday night to myself.
What if I leave early Saturday?
That is still staying over. I am not going to relitigate this one.
Okay. I did not mean to push.
I know. I am telling you clearly so you do not have to guess.
Saturday afternoon then?
Saturday afternoon works. Thank you for hearing the no.

threads.title: Checking whether a yes is real
threads.note: She does not count a reluctant yes as agreement.

bubbles.text: You said yes to meeting my friends, but you went quiet after. Is that a real yes?
It is fine. I am just nervous.
Nervous is allowed. I would rather you say no than come and resent it.
I do want to meet them. I just do not want to be grilled.
Then I will tell them to keep it light. That is a thing I can offer.
That helps.
Good. If it stops feeling fine, tell me before the day, not after.

threads.title: When the terms do not match
threads.note: She accepts that a mismatch can end the conversation without a villain.

bubbles.text: I think I want something more casual than you do.
That is useful to know. I want to see someone regularly, and casual does not fit that for me.
I do not want to waste your time.
Then we are not wasting it. We are just finding out early.
Are you angry?
No. I am disappointed, and that is mine to handle. You do not have to manage it.
Okay. I am sorry it is not a match.
Me too. I would rather know now than in three months.

characters.name: Samantha Jones
characters.why: In Sex and the City, Samantha Jones states what she wants from a relationship plainly and declines arrangements that do not suit her, which is the Deal Broker move of naming terms instead of hinting.

characters.name: Miranda Hobbes
characters.why: Miranda Hobbes in Sex and the City tends to put her actual availability and limits on the table, including when a partner's expectations do not fit, rather than pretending the mismatch is not there.

characters.name: Leslie Knope
characters.why: Leslie Knope in Parks and Recreation negotiates plans and commitments with explicit offers and asks, which matches the habit of spelling out what each side is putting in.

characters.name: Cristina Yang
characters.why: Cristina Yang in Grey's Anatomy says what she will and will not give in a relationship, and the Deal Broker pattern shows in her treating those limits as settled rather than as a debate to win.

closest_cousin.text: Bringing two relatives back to the same table takes bridge building. Brokering an agreement might come later, when she asks whether one can do the school pickup in exchange for the other covering the evening shift.
closest_cousin.tell: Look at what the conversation produced. Did they reopen contact, or did each person also accept a specific part of an exchange?

interested.point: She names the offer out loud
interested.detail: After two good dates she says, "I want to keep seeing you weekly-ish and stay exclusive while we figure this out. Is that something you'd actually want, or are you picturing something looser?" You never have to guess whether her warmth was politeness or intent because she puts the terms in plain words.

interested.point: Voluntary means voluntary
interested.detail: She asks whether Saturday works, then adds, "If you'd rather keep weekends for your own people, say so and we'll find a weeknight." When you take the weeknight, she doesn't treat it as a test you passed. She treats it as the answer.

interested.point: She asks what would settle it
interested.detail: Mid-disagreement about how often to text, she asks, "What would actually make this feel resolved for you?" then offers her own version: "I'd call it settled if we each reply within a day and neither of us keeps score." It moves the argument from mood to a concrete finish line.

interested.point: Walking away is allowed
interested.detail: When you say the timeline she wants is faster than you can move, she says, "Okay. Then that's a real mismatch, and I'd rather we both know now." She doesn't punish you for declining and doesn't chase. She means the exit is available to both of you.

interested.point: She separates preferences from limits
interested.detail: She can say "I'd prefer you meet my friends soon" in one breath and "I won't stay in a situation where plans get cancelled last minute" in another, and the difference is audible. The preference has room for a no. The limit has already been decided.

interested.point: Terms get rechecked, not assumed
interested.detail: A month in, she says, "We agreed to check back on the holidays. Does that offer still stand, or has it changed?" She assumes people change their minds without it being betrayal. You can revise a yes without a fight.

not_interested.point: She reads terms as an ultimatum
not_interested.detail: When she says, "Here's what I'm offering and here's what I need," you hear a courtroom and brace for a verdict. The content might have suited you, but the framing feels like pressure and you shut down before considering it.

not_interested.point: You want implication over spelling out
not_interested.detail: You prefer people to read the room and let things develop without a stated agreement. Her check-in texts about where a relationship is heading feel clinical, and you'd rather not put things into words that early.

not_interested.point: You thought a stated limit was negotiable
not_interested.detail: You treated her "I don't do on-again off-again" as an opening bid and pushed for a trial separation. She restated it once, then stepped back, and you found that abrupt rather than fair.

not_interested.point: Asking about consent feels like distrust
not_interested.detail: She asks before changing something you'd agreed to, including small things like whether you're still comfortable with overnight stays. You experience the question as her doubting you, and the repeated asking wears on you.

not_interested.point: She won't bid against herself
not_interested.detail: You liked that she was direct until she declined to keep improving her offer while you stalled. Her "that's my position, take it or leave it" felt cold, when from her side it was simply not bargaining with herself.

not_interested.point: Her calm reads as distance
not_interested.detail: You want someone who reacts strongly and pushes back hard when hurt. Her steady "I'm not going to argue about this, but I'm not agreeing either" feels like withdrawal, even though she stays in the conversation.

red_flags.point: Terms only cut one way
red_flags.detail: She lists what you owe in detail and greets your requests with "let's not be transactional." Noticing the asymmetry is fair. You don't owe her a one-sided agreement just because she calls it honesty.

red_flags.point: Consent treated as a formality
red_flags.detail: She frames "I already said yes once" as covering every later ask and sulks when you check again. A yes to one thing is not a standing lease on your body or time, and pushing past that is not dealmaking.

red_flags.point: Boundaries reopened after each no
red_flags.detail: She accepts a limit in the moment and returns to it days later with new arguments and a hurt tone. Reopening a settled no, again and again, is pressure dressed as persistence.

red_flags.point: The scoreboard
red_flags.detail: She keeps a running tally of who compromised more and produces it during unrelated conflicts. Reciprocity becomes leverage, and you start pre-paying favors to avoid the next audit.

red_flags.point: Walk-away used as threat
red_flags.detail: She floats leaving whenever she wants a concession, then says she was only being honest about her options. A real exit is fine. A recurring threat to get your compliance is not a term you should accept.

red_flags.point: Confidential terms
red_flags.detail: She asks you to keep the arrangement private from friends who would ask fair questions, calling it "just between us." Secrecy about the basics of a relationship is a signal to slow down, not a sign of intimacy.

green_flags.point: Both sides get a draft
green_flags.detail: She states her terms and then asks, "What's your version, and where does mine not work for you?" She waits for your answer before treating anything as agreed. You leave the conversation knowing exactly what each of you said yes to.

green_flags.point: The right to leave stays intact
green_flags.detail: She says plainly that either of you can end things without a trial, and she doesn't withdraw warmth to punish the option. Knowing the exit is real makes staying feel chosen rather than trapped.

green_flags.point: Small asks get real answers
green_flags.detail: She checks in before changing plans, including small ones, and accepts "not tonight" without a debate. Consent here is a habit rather than a hurdle, and refusals don't cost you affection.

green_flags.point: She keeps her own no
green_flags.detail: When you push for something she's declined, she says, "I hear you, and my answer is still no," without insulting you. Her consistency signals she'll defend your limits with the same steadiness.

green_flags.point: The matter gets closed
green_flags.detail: Once you both agree, she names what would count as done and stops re-litigating. You can tell when a question is settled because she treats it as settled, which leaves room for the parts of the relationship that aren't negotiations.

what_to_say.line: Here is what I am offering: I can do Saturday evenings and I can text during the day, but I am not available after ten at night.
what_to_say.why: Naming the actual terms, including hours, makes the offer checkable instead of atmospheric. He can say yes, ask for a change, or say it does not work, and any of those answers is usable.

what_to_say.line: This part is negotiable. That part is not. Tell me which one you are answering.
what_to_say.why: Separating flexible terms from fixed ones keeps a conversation from turning into a package deal where one no collapses everything. It also gives him a clean way to decline half without rejecting you.

what_to_say.line: If we cannot agree on this, I would rather we stop here as friends than keep renegotiating it every month.
what_to_say.why: Stating the outcome of no agreement beforehand makes walking away a known option rather than a threat produced mid-argument. It respects his time and yours.

what_to_say.line: I want to check that this is a real yes and not a polite one. What would make this easier for you?
what_to_say.why: Consent asked as a question about conditions, not a box to tick, invites an honest answer. It also signals that a no will not be treated as an opening bid.

what_to_say.line: I noticed I said yes to that last week and I actually meant maybe. Can we redo that part?
what_to_say.why: Correcting your own terms out loud models that the table is honest and revisable. It gives him permission to revise his answers too without it counting as a betrayal.

never_say.line: If you really cared, you would not need terms.
never_say.why: This turns a request for clarity into a test of feeling and makes agreement the price of affection. He may agree just to prove himself, which produces a yes nobody can trust.

never_say.line: I have written down what you are giving me. Sign off on it tonight.
never_say.why: A same-night signature under pressure is not consent, it is compliance. Real terms survive a night of thinking and a conversation with someone he trusts.

never_say.line: My boundary is that you never see your friends on weekends.
never_say.why: Calling a demand a boundary blurs the line between your limits and his life. A boundary describes what you will do, not what he is forbidden to do.

never_say.line: You said yes, so it is settled forever.
never_say.why: Treating one yes as permanent removes his right to change his mind, which is the core of consent. Terms need a review date, especially early on.

never_say.line: Fine, I will just accept whatever you want and stop asking.
never_say.why: Withdrawing your own terms to avoid friction creates a false agreement he never actually made. Resentment arrives later disguised as his fault.

manipulation.name: The Bundled Offer
manipulation.how_it_works: A desirable term is tied to a costly one so declining the cost looks like rejecting the whole offer. He ends up agreeing to something he never separately considered.
manipulation.defense: Ask to split the bundle and answer each term alone. A real offer survives being taken apart and answered piece by piece.

manipulation.name: The Moving Baseline
manipulation.how_it_works: Each time he agrees, a new condition appears before the old one is honored. The table keeps shifting so he is always one yes behind.
manipulation.defense: Write the agreed terms down once and treat additions as a fresh conversation with a fresh yes. If the list grows every week, name the pattern and pause.

manipulation.name: The Sympathy Discount
manipulation.how_it_works: A hard week or a past hurt is introduced right before a request so declining feels cruel. The ask is framed as comfort rather than a term.
manipulation.defense: Separate care from agreement: offer comfort now and discuss the ask tomorrow. A term that only works when he feels guilty is not one he chose.

manipulation.name: The Audit
manipulation.how_it_works: Past favors are tallied and presented as debts owed at the table. Generosity becomes a ledger he is expected to settle with new commitments.
manipulation.defense: Say plainly that gifts are not deposits and ask which current term is actually in question. Keep the conversation on what is being decided now.

manipulation.name: The Trial Balloon
manipulation.how_it_works: A serious term is floated as a joke or a maybe to test his reaction without owning the ask. Deniability lets her retreat if he resists.
manipulation.defense: Ask whether this is a real proposal before responding to it. Only real proposals deserve answers and only owned asks can be declined cleanly.

leverage.point: Set a review date
leverage.detail: Agree that you will both revisit the terms in four weeks. A scheduled review turns a fixed deal into a living one and gives either of you a safe moment to change an answer.

leverage.point: Name your walk-away point first
leverage.detail: Before the conversation, decide what would make you leave the table and say it once, calmly. Knowing your own exit makes the negotiation honest rather than desperate.

leverage.point: Ask for his terms, not just his yes
leverage.detail: Invite him to put his own conditions on the table before you finalize anything. A deal where only one side states terms is a request, not an agreement.

leverage.point: Keep consent revisable
leverage.detail: Tell him explicitly that any yes can become a no later without penalty. This protects the deal from becoming a cage and makes later honesty more likely.

leverage.point: Check the deal against your own limit
leverage.detail: After agreeing, ask yourself whether you accepted because it suited you or because the room was tense. If it was tension, say so and reopen that term.

proceduralist-her.identity: She gets agreement on how to decide while everyone can still influence the rules.
summary: She treats a disputed decision as a design problem before it becomes a loyalty test. When you are dating her, she may say, before either of you knows who will get the apartment or which family gets the holiday, 'Here is how we will decide, here is how we will know it worked, and here is when we can reopen it.' That is the Co-Builder at work: she is not handing you a ballot and calling it partnership.

The procedure she proposes is specific enough to check later. She names who gets a say, what counts as a say, who breaks a tie, and what evidence would tell either of you the outcome needs a second look. If you ask her what happens if one of you hates the result, she has an answer ready, such as a scheduled review on a set date rather than a vague promise to talk.

She is not allergic to disagreement. She is allergic to discovering the rules after the result. So she will pause a heated conversation long enough to ask whether you both agree on the question, the inputs and the deadline, and she will write it down if you are both tired. She also expects you to push back on her proposed rules, and she notices when you do not.

Her style can wear thin if the process becomes the point. A couple who plans a two-hour meeting to decide where to eat is not co-building, it is stalling. The healthy version leaves room for someone to say, 'Actually, forget the framework, I just want Thai,' and for the other person to agree without a procedural appeal.

text: Her texts often arrive as compact proposals with a hook for your consent. She might send, 'Before we book the trip, can we agree that whoever has the nonrefundable work conflict wins, and the other person gets first pick next time? If we still disagree Friday, I will call it and we review in a month.' The message is not a demand, it is an invitation to amend the rules while the stakes are low.

She also uses texts to make the outcome checkable. After a decision she may write, 'We said we would know by June whether the shorter commute was worth it. Want to put a coffee on the calendar for the 15th and actually look at the numbers?' If you reply with a flat yes, expect a gentle follow-up question about whether you meant the process or just wanted the conversation to end.

threads.title: Choosing a shared apartment
threads.note: She separates the decision rule from the listing she happens to like, which keeps a disagreement about rent from becoming a verdict on the relationship.

bubbles.text: Before we tour anything, can we agree on the tiebreak if we love different places?
You mean like a coin flip?
Not quite. We each rank our top three, compare lists, and if there is no overlap whoever has the shorter commute gets one extra point.
And if I think the commute rule is dumb?
Then say so now and we will swap it before we sign anything. I do not want to hear about it after we move in.
Fair. I would rather weight the budget more than the commute.
Okay. Budget first, commute second, and we revisit in six months with actual receipts.

threads.title: Holiday with both families
threads.note: The fair revisit is scheduled before the first holiday, so neither person has to weaponize a bad afternoon later.

bubbles.text: My mom already assumed we are doing Thanksgiving at her place.
I figured something like that would happen. Can we decide the rule instead of the dinner?
What rule?
Alternate years, with a swap allowed if someone asks by October 1. If we cannot agree on a swap, the original plan stands.
And if the swap turns out awful?
We put a check-in on the calendar for January and talk about whether to keep the rule. No surprise ambush at Christmas.
Okay, but I want to be able to say the swap was a mistake without it becoming a fight about your family.
That is exactly what the January check-in is for.

threads.title: Splitting a big purchase
threads.note: They set a spending rule together. When the sale puts pressure on the deadline, she honors the other person’s request for a day to think.

bubbles.text: The couch is on sale until Sunday. I do not want to buy it just because the timer is ticking.
I thought you loved it.
I do. But we said anything over five hundred gets two yeses. Do you have a yes in you?
I have a maybe. I want to sit on it for a day.
Then we wait. If we miss the sale, we miss it.
What if we disagree tomorrow?
We each write one sentence about why, swap, and if we still disagree we keep the old couch and revisit in three months.

threads.title: Revisiting a decision that went badly
threads.note: This is the test of whether the procedure was real: she opens the review she agreed to instead of defending the original call.

bubbles.text: The dinner party rule is not working. I spent an hour mediating between your friend and mine.
We said we would review it after three dinners. This is number three, so you are right on time.
I want to scrap the seating chart.
Okay. What should replace it, and who decides if we disagree on the replacement?
I do not know yet. Can we each bring one option to coffee Saturday?
Yes. And if we cannot pick by then, we go back to open seating for one dinner and try again.
I can live with that.
Good. I would rather change the rule than pretend the party was fine.

characters.name: Leslie Knope
characters.why: Leslie Knope in Parks and Recreation builds agendas and public processes for ordinary decisions, and she expects the people around her to amend the agenda rather than sulk about it afterward.

characters.name: Dana Scully
characters.why: Dana Scully in The X-Files insists on evidence and a reviewable chain of reasoning before accepting a conclusion, which mirrors the Proceduralist's insistence that an outcome be checkable.

characters.name: Tami Taylor
characters.why: Tami Taylor in Friday Night Lights negotiates concrete rules with her partner and revisits them when circumstances change, showing the Co-Builder style in a family setting rather than a courtroom one.

characters.name: Kim Wexler
characters.why: Kim Wexler in Better Call Saul works through disputed plans by naming who decides and what gets reviewed, and she keeps the terms explicit even when the other person would rather improvise.

closest_cousin.text: When two friends plan a holiday, they can both choose stops and activities. A different contribution is to agree in advance on a private spending ceiling, two yeses for an expensive booking and a deadline after which either can revisit the plan.
closest_cousin.tell: Listen for the moment she asks how the two of you will break a tie. Check whether she also follows that agreement when her first choice loses.

interested.point: She names the decider before the stakes land
interested.detail: On a Tuesday call about whose apartment to move into, she asks whether you want to decide jointly or give one person the call with a review date. She writes the answer in the shared note before either of you has toured a single place.

interested.point: Tie rules exist before disagreement
interested.detail: She suggests that if you split on a restaurant for a birthday, the person whose occasion it is breaks the tie. She brings this up over coffee, not when you are already hungry and late.

interested.point: She treats a vote as a tool, not a verdict
interested.detail: When you both rank three weekend plans, she notices the ranking hides how much you care about one of them. She asks whether the top two should get a longer conversation instead of a straight count.

interested.point: Revisiting has a door and a date
interested.detail: After agreeing to spend holidays separately this year, she proposes checking the decision in March when schedules are clearer. She asks what would count as a reason to reopen it, and you both name one.

interested.point: She separates the process from the person
interested.detail: You forget to log your preference in the shared doc she made, and she says the missed entry is a process gap, not a character flaw. Then she asks if the doc is too much work and offers to drop it.

interested.point: She asks about consent to the method
interested.detail: Before proposing a coin flip for who calls the plumber, she asks whether randomness feels fine to you or whether you would rather trade off. She accepts a no without treating it as resistance.

not_interested.point: She wants the outcome settled now, not the method
not_interested.detail: When you ask how you two should decide on a shared trip budget, she says let us just pick something and move on. She gets restless when you try to name who has the final word.

not_interested.point: Written agreements feel like paperwork to her
not_interested.detail: You suggest a short note about how you will handle future disagreements over chores, and she says that turns a relationship into a contract. She would rather trust the mood of the moment.

not_interested.point: She hears a tie rule as distrust
not_interested.detail: You propose that if you cannot agree on a movie, you alternate who chooses. She says planning for a tie means you expect conflict, and the evening deflates.

not_interested.point: She dislikes review dates
not_interested.detail: After you both agree on a budget for gifts this year, she resists setting a check-in because it feels like an audit. She prefers to leave it open and adjust if it comes up.

not_interested.point: She wants one person to own every plan
not_interested.detail: She says one of you should just be in charge of social calendars and the other should go along. When you ask about switching who decides, she calls the question overcomplicated.

not_interested.point: She reads a checklist as coldness
not_interested.detail: You offer a two line list of who books what for the move, and she says you are managing her instead of helping. She would rather improvise on the day and sort out confusion later.

red_flags.point: The method changes after the result
red_flags.detail: You agree that the lower bid on the used couch wins, and when her bid loses she says the process was never really fair. She proposes a new rule only once she dislikes the outcome.

red_flags.point: She names you as the decider then punishes the call
red_flags.detail: She tells you to choose the vacation spot and says she is fine with anything. When you pick, she brings it up for weeks as evidence you do not consider her.

red_flags.point: She uses the process to dodge her own preference
red_flags.detail: She insists on a neutral tie breaker for weekend plans, then sulks when the coin sends you to your choice. She will not say what she actually wanted before the toss.

red_flags.point: Reopening becomes endless
red_flags.detail: Every agreed review date turns into a full renegotiation of the original decision with new conditions. She never lets a settled outcome stand long enough for either of you to test it.

red_flags.point: She treats your request for a review date as betrayal
red_flags.detail: You ask to check in on a joint decision in a month, and she says you are already planning the exit. She refuses to name any condition under which the decision could change.

red_flags.point: She records consent as a weapon
red_flags.detail: She gets you to agree to a method in a rushed moment, then quotes it later to shut down your hesitation. When you say the agreement no longer fits, she calls you inconsistent rather than reopening it.

green_flags.point: She writes the tie rule in plain words
green_flags.detail: Before you pick a shared streaming account or split a bill, she types one sentence about who decides if you disagree. She reads it back and asks if it matches what you understood.

green_flags.point: She offers a fair revisit clause
green_flags.detail: After agreeing to alternate who plans date night, she suggests either person can call a review after three turns. She names what would count as a reason to change the rhythm, such as one person always planning the expensive option.

green_flags.point: She checks whether the method fits the stakes
green_flags.detail: For a low stakes choice like takeout, she is fine with a quick coin flip. For a lease, she asks for a longer conversation and a written note of who decides what, showing she does not apply one tool everywhere.

green_flags.point: She distinguishes a no from an attack
green_flags.detail: When you decline her proposed voting app for household decisions, she asks what would feel workable instead. She does not push the app again or frame your no as sabotage.

green_flags.point: She names her own preference before the process starts
green_flags.detail: She says she leans toward the cheaper apartment but still wants a clear method for the final call. That way the procedure is not a hiding place for what she already wants.

what_to_say.line: Before we pick a restaurant for Friday, do you want to alternate who chooses, or should we each name two and flip a coin if they don't overlap?
what_to_say.why: It names two workable procedures and asks her to pick one before the outcome exists; that invites co-ownership instead of testing whether she guesses your preference.

what_to_say.line: If we can't agree on the couch by Sunday, I'd like to set a two-week trial and decide at the end whether to keep it or return it. Does that feel fair to you?
what_to_say.why: A trial with a review date is a real procedure, not a vague promise to talk later; it gives both people an exit and a checkable moment.

what_to_say.line: I want to say how I'd like us to handle this before I tell you what I want, so neither of us feels cornered. Is that okay?
what_to_say.why: Ordering the conversation protects the smaller-voice person and makes the process visible; asking consent keeps it from becoming a unilateral rule.

what_to_say.line: Last month we agreed you'd book the flights and I'd handle the hotel. I booked mine. Do you want to keep that split or trade one part?
what_to_say.why: It references a specific prior agreement and checks it against reality without accusation; the trade offer keeps the arrangement revisable.

what_to_say.line: When we disagreed about the party, you suggested a coin flip and I want to try that next time, but can we agree that either of us can ask for a redo after a week?
what_to_say.why: It credits a concrete mechanism and adds a fair revisit clause; the redo option means the procedure itself is open to adjustment.

never_say.line: Just tell me what you want and I'll go along with it.
never_say.why: That sounds accommodating but quietly hands her all the decisions and later resentment; it gives her no partner in building the plan. Say instead which parts you want a say in.

never_say.line: We decided this already, so there's nothing to discuss.
never_say.why: Closure without a revisit path turns a past agreement into a trap; name when and how the decision can be reopened.

never_say.line: If you really cared, you'd let me handle it my way.
never_say.why: It swaps a process question for a loyalty test and makes disagreement costly; separate care from agreement on method.

never_say.line: I don't do votes. I just know what's right.
never_say.why: Claiming special insight skips the agreement about how decisions get made; offer a method and let her accept or counter it.

never_say.line: Fine, we'll do it your way, but don't expect me to be happy.
never_say.why: Compliance with a side of punishment makes the next agreement harder; say plainly whether you consent and what you need changed.

manipulation.name: The Moving Goalpost
manipulation.how_it_works: After a vote or coin flip she dislikes, she reframes the question so the earlier result no longer counts. That erodes trust in any agreed procedure and leaves the other person unsure what was settled.
manipulation.defense: Before deciding, write down the exact question being settled and the result. If someone redefines it afterward, ask whether they want to reopen the whole agreement rather than relitigate the old one.

manipulation.name: The Secret Tiebreaker
manipulation.how_it_works: She agrees to a process but keeps an unstated veto, such as claiming the final call as host or elder. The other person discovers the rule only when it blocks them.
manipulation.defense: Ask directly who breaks a tie and what makes that person eligible, then repeat it back. If a new authority appears midstream, pause and renegotiate the rule in plain terms.

manipulation.name: The Checklist Theater
manipulation.how_it_works: She produces an elaborate shared document that looks fair but is designed so every path leads to her preferred outcome. The format substitutes for genuine consent.
manipulation.defense: Test the checklist on a case where you would lose. If the same person wins every branch, the procedure is decoration and deserves a rewrite.

manipulation.name: The Soft Deadline
manipulation.how_it_works: She keeps extending the review date so an outcome never becomes checkable, and the other person is left waiting indefinitely. Delay becomes a way to avoid accountability.
manipulation.defense: Put a specific date and consequence in the agreement, such as a default if no review happens. Treat repeated extensions as information about whether the plan is real.

manipulation.name: The Revisit Loop
manipulation.how_it_works: Using the fair idea of revisiting, she reopens settled decisions so often that nothing holds and the other person tires into conceding. The right to review becomes a pressure tool.
manipulation.defense: Limit revisits to a stated interval or a material change in facts. Name what new information would justify reopening and decline repeats that offer none.

leverage.point: Name your preferred decision method first
leverage.detail: Say whether you want a vote, alternating turns, or a coin flip before stating your position on the issue. Choosing the method early keeps the procedure from being reverse-engineered around a preferred answer.

leverage.point: Ask for a written tie and review clause
leverage.detail: Write one sentence covering who decides a tie and when the outcome gets a check-in. A visible clause makes the promise testable in the moment, not just in memory.

leverage.point: Use a reversible trial instead of a permanent win
leverage.detail: For contested purchases or plans, propose a two-week trial with a set review date. The trial keeps disagreement from becoming a permanent verdict and gives both people a clean exit.

leverage.point: Decline a process you did not agree to
leverage.detail: If a checklist or vote appears after the fact, say you did not consent to that method and offer to build one together. Refusing an imposed process is not obstruction, it is protecting shared control.

leverage.point: Ask who benefits from each branch
leverage.detail: Walk through the agreed procedure on a case where you would lose. If the same person wins every path, name that pattern and propose a change before the next decision.
